q: Why can a rising serum creatinine be pathological even when it remains near the laboratory normal range?
o: A value at the upper limit of normal excludes significant loss of renal function
Serum creatinine should rise with normal aging and need not affect renal drug dosing
Creatinine production increases as muscle mass falls, so a rising level is normal aging
Muscle loss reduces creatinine production, so serum creatinine should remain relatively constant
explanation:
Loss of muscle mass reduces creatinine production, so serum creatinine should remain relatively constant and an upper-normal level can reflect important renal decline (p1268).

C. Creatinine production increases as muscle mass falls, so a rising level is normal aging: The book describes reduced creatinine production with loss of muscle mass (p1268).
A. A value at the upper limit of normal excludes significant loss of renal function: The book states that an upper-normal level can represent significant decline in an older individual (p1268).
B. Serum creatinine should rise with normal aging and need not affect renal drug dosing: The book says creatinine should remain relatively constant and elevations warrant attention to renal function and dosing (p1268).

q: Is proteinuria an expected consequence of normal human aging?
o: No - proteinuria is always pathological and requires a full work-up
No - proteinuria needs no work-up when creatinine stays in its normal range
Yes - normal age-related GFR decline makes proteinuria expected
Yes - proteinuria is normal in aging humans as it is in rats
explanation:
Proteinuria is not a normal feature of human kidney aging and requires a full work-up (p1269).

D. Yes - proteinuria is normal in aging humans as it is in rats: The book explicitly distinguishes humans from rodent models (p1269).
C. Yes - normal age-related GFR decline makes proteinuria expected: Despite declining GFR, proteinuria is not a normal feature of aging (p1269).
B. No - proteinuria needs no work-up when creatinine stays in its normal range: The book requires a work-up of proteinuria; an upper-normal creatinine can itself reflect significant loss of function (p1269; p1268).

q: As GFR declines, how does potassium fractional excretion differ in older versus younger adults?
o: The fractional excretion of potassium does not rise as much as in young individuals
It rises more than in young individuals because aldosterone levels increase
A smaller fractional-excretion rise usually makes unstressed serum potassium abnormal
The fractional-excretion rise is similar in younger and older adults despite declining GFR
explanation: Older adults can have normal potassium under unstressed conditions; as GFR declines, fractional potassium excretion rises less than in younger people, partly because of lower aldosterone or resistance (p1270). An increased rise due to increased aldosterone, abnormal unstressed potassium as the consequence, and equal age responses are wrong.

q: Does absence of typical ECG changes exclude dangerous hyperkalemia?
o: No - absence of ECG findings does not make hyperkalemia erroneous or insignificant
No - a given potassium level usually produces the same ECG pattern across patients
Yes - the classic sequence of ECG changes is the usual pattern of dangerous hyperkalemia
Yes - an absent ECG pattern generally establishes that the potassium result is erroneous
explanation: The classic progression of hyperkalemic ECG changes is seldom seen; absent ECG findings do not mean hyperkalemia is erroneous or insignificant (p1271). The same level producing a usual fixed pattern, the classic sequence being usual, and absent findings establishing error all contradict this warning.

q: What makes podocyte loss important in the proposed sclerosis mechanism?
o: These specialized cells are postmitotic and if damaged in any way, cannot be replaced.
The proposed mechanism preserves every nephron despite complete glomerular sclerosis
Podocyte detachment leaves the filtration barrier fully covered and prevents sclerosis
Podocytes multiply in proportion to glomerular tuft enlargement
explanation:
Podocytes are postmitotic and cannot be replaced. Their detachment with tuft expansion is believed to expose basement membrane and initiate sclerosis (p1272).

D. Podocytes multiply in proportion to glomerular tuft enlargement: Unlike endothelial and mesangial cells, podocytes cannot multiply to match increasing tuft volume (p1272).
C. Podocyte detachment leaves the filtration barrier fully covered and prevents sclerosis: Detachment exposes basement membrane and is thought to trigger sclerosis (p1272).
B. The proposed mechanism preserves every nephron despite complete glomerular sclerosis: An entire glomerulus can sclerose and shrivel with loss of that nephron and filtration capacity (p1272).

q: Does the chapter establish protein restriction as prevention of normal human kidney aging?
o: No - protein restriction tends to worsen symptoms in established uremia
Yes - lower-protein vegetarians had better-preserved kidney function than meat eaters
Yes - animal studies establish prevention of normal human kidney aging
No - evidence supports uremic symptom reduction, not prevention of human kidney aging
explanation: The described vegetarian and meat-eating groups did not differ in kidney function. Protein restriction has evidence for reducing uremic symptoms in established renal disease, not for preventing age-related human kidney changes (p1274). Worsening uremic symptoms, a vegetarian renal-preservation advantage, and extrapolating animal evidence to established human prevention are wrong.
